DOSAGE FORMS USED IN UTTARA BASTI

1, Taila: Example: Kshirabala Taila - This medicinal
oil contains Bala (Sida cordifolia) and Kshira (milk),
among other herbs. It is beneficial in conditions
like urinary tract infections, kidney stones, and
male reproductive disorders such as premature
ejaculation.

2. Ghrita; Example: Yoni Prakshalana Ghrita -
This medicinal ghee is prepared from Sariva
(Hemidesmus indicus) and Daruharidra (Berberis
aristata), among other ingredients. It is beneficial in
conditions related to menstrual disorders, vaginal
infections, and female infertility.

| 9.8 Yoni Marga

YONI DHARANA
INTRODUCTION

Yoni Dharana is an Ayurvedic therapeutic procedure
that involves applying herbal pastes or poultices to
the vaginal area (Yoni). It is a specialized form of local
treatment aimed at addressing various gynecological
issues, promoting reproductive health, and providing
relief from discomfort or inflammation in the genital
region.

----- PAGE 269 -----
Chapter 9 + Aushadhi Prayoga Marga

NEED FOR YONI DHARANA

Yoni Dharana is utilized in cases of synecological
disorders such as vaginal infections, inflammation
itching, and discharge. It is also beneficial for promoting
overall vaginal health, maintaining PH balance, and
supporting reproductive function. Yoni Dharana
provides targeted relief and healing to the delicate
tissues of the vagina, addressing specific concerns
related to hygiene, comfort, and well-being.

BENEFITS OF YONI DHARANA

. Relief from Vaginal Infections: Herbal pastes used
in Yoni Dharana have antimicrobial, antifungal,
and anti-inflammatory properties, which help
combat infections such as bacterial vaginosis, yeast
infections, and urinary tract infections.

. Soothing Irritation and Itching: Yoni Dharana helps
soothe irritation, itching, and discomfort in the
vaginal area, providing immediate relief and
promoting healing of inflamed tissues.

. Maintaining Vaginal pH Balance: Certain herbal
formulations used in Yoni Dharana help maintain
the natural pH balance of the vagina, preventing
the overgrowth of harmful microorganisms and
reducing the risk of infections.

4. Supporting Reproductive Health: Yoni Dharana is
beneficial for women experiencing menstrual
irregularities, vaginal dryness, or discomfort during
intercourse. It helps promote lubrication, improve
blood circulation, and support overall reproductive
health.

5. Postpartum Care: Yoni Dharana is often
recommended as part of postpartum care to

romote healing and soothe the vaginal area after
childbirth. It helps reduce inflammation, prevent
infections, and alleviate discomfort associated with
episiotomy or perineal tears.

EXAMPLES OF HERBAL FORMULATIONS FOR YONI DHARANA:

1. Yoni Prakshalana Churna: A herbal powder
formulation containing ingredients like Triphala,
Neem, and Lodhra, used for cleansing and
detoxifying the vaginal area.

2. Yoni Prakshalana Ghrita: A medicated ghee prepared
with herb like Sariva, Daruharidra, and Manjistha,
used for soothing inflammation, promoting healing,
and maintaining vaginal health.

. Yoni Kalka: Herbal pastes prepared with ingredients
like Haridra, Nimba, and Yashtimadhu, used
for relieving itching, reducing discharge, and
combating infections.

YONI DHAVANA

Yoni Dhavana is an Ayurvedic practice that involves
washing or cleansing the vaginal area (Yoni) with herbal
decoctions or infusions. It is a traditional method used
to maintain vaginal hygiene, promote reproductive
health, and alleviate discomfort or symptoms associated
with various gynecological conditions.

NEED FoR Yon) DHAVANA

Yoni Dhavana is recommended for women experiencing
vaginal infections, inflammation, itching, excessive
discharge, or discomfort during menstruation. It
helps to cleanse the vaginal area, remove impurities,
and restore the natural balance of the vaginal flora.
Yoni Dhavana isalso beneficial for women seeking to
maintain overall vaginal health and hygiene.

BENEFITS OF YONI DHAVANA

1. Cleansing and Purification: Herbal decoctions used
in Yoni Dhavana have cleansing and purifying
properties, helping to remove dirt, bacteria, and
toxins from the vaginal area.

- Relief from Infections: Yoni Dhavana helps to alleviate
symptoms of vaginal infections such as itching,
burning, and unusual discharge by promoting a
healthy vaginal environment and inhibiting the
growth of harmful microorganisms.

3. Reduction of Inflammation: The soothing and anti-
inflammatory properties of herbal decoctions used
in Yoni Dhavana help to reduce inflammation and
swelling in the vaginal tissues, providing relief
from discomfort.

. Regulation of pH Balance: Yoni Dhavana helps to
maintain the natural pH balance of the vagina,
which is essential for preventing the over growth
of harmful bacteria and yeast that can lead to
infections.

5. Support for Menstrual Health: Yoni Dhavana may
help to alleviate menstrual cramps, discomfort, and
excessive bleeding by promoting relaxation and
improving blood circulation in the pelvic area.

(10.1 Introduction

The National Accreditation Board for Hospitals &
Healthcare Providers (NABH) sets comprehensive
guidelines to improve healthcare quality and ensure
patient safety in India. These guidelines encompass
various aspects of healthcare delivery, including rational
prescription and safe dispensing of medications, which
are crucial for preventing medication errors, optimizing
patient outcomes, and promoting efficient healthcare
delivery. When applied to Ayurvedic formulations,
these guidelines help integrate traditional practices
with modern standards of care, ensuring holistic and
safe patient treatment.

40.2 Rational Prescription

1. DEFINITION AND IMPORTANCE

Rational prescription involves the use of medications
that are appropriate to the patient's clinical needs, in
doses that meet their requirements, for an adequate
period, and at the lowest cost to them and their
community. This approach aims to ensure that patients
receive the most effective treatment while minimizing
the risk of adverse effects and medication errors. In
Ayurveda, this means selecting formulations that are
best suited to the patient’s unique constitution (Prakriti)
and disease condition (Vyadhi).

2. KEY GUIDELINES

NABH emphasizes several core principles for rational
prescription:

% Evidence-Based Prescribing:

e Physicians are encouraged to prescribe medications
based on the best available scientific evidence,
considering the effectiveness, safety, and cost.

e In Ayurveda, this includes using classical texts,
recent research, and clinical experience to guide
prescription.

RATIONAL PRESCRIPTION ALONG WITH SAFE
DISPENSING OF AYURVEDIC FORMULATIONS

“+ Patient-Centered Care

e Prescriptions should be tailored to individual
patient needs, considering factors such as age,
gender, co-morbidities, and allergies.

e In Ayurveda, this involves a thorough assessment
of the patient’s Dosha imbalance and Prakriti.

“- Comprehensive Documentation:

e Detailed documentation of prescribed
medications, including dosage, frequency, and
duration, is mandatory.

e In Ayurvedic practice, this includes documenting
the rationale for choosing specific formulations
and treatments based on patient assessment.

“ Regular Review and Monitoring:

e Periodic review of the patient's medication
regimen is recommended to assess efficacy and
make necessary adjustments.

e Monitoring for adverse drug reactions and
ensuring patient adherence to the prescribed
regimen are critical.

10.3 Safe Dispensing

1. DEFINITION AND IMPORTANCE

Safe dispensing involves the accurate preparation and
distribution of medications, ensuring that patients
receive the correct drugs in the appropriate dosage and
form. This process is vital for preventing dispensing
errors, which can lead to significant patient harm.

2. KEY GUIDELINES
NABH sets forth guidelines to enhance the safety and
accuracy of the dispensing process:
+ Qualified Personnel
e Dispensing should be performed by qualified
pharmacists or trained personnel under their
supervision.

----- PAGE 274 -----
260

Rasashastra and Bhaishajya Kalpana * Chapter 10

¢ In Ayurvedic practice, this may involve trained
Ayurvedic pharmacists and practitioners.

ENSURING PATIENTSAFETY AND IMPROVING HEALTHCARE QUALITY

1. Prevention of Medication Errors: By adhering to
NABH guidelines, healthcare provi-ders can signifi-
cantly reduce the risk of medication errors. Rational
prescribing practices ensure that patien’= receive
appropriate medications, while safe d. ensing
protocols prevent errors during the medication
preparation and distribution process.

2. Optimizing Patient Outcomes: Rational prescription
and safe dispensing practices contribute to better
patient outcomes by ensuring that patients receive
effective and safe treatments tailored to their
individual needs. Regular monitoring and patient
education further enhance treatment efficacy and
adherence.

3. Enhancing Healthcare Efficiency: Following NABH
guidelines promotes efficient use of healthcare
resources by minimizing wastage, reducing
adverse drug reactions, and preventing hospital
readmissions due to medication-related issues. This
efficiency ultimately contributes to cost savings for
both patients and healthcare systems.

4. Building Patient Trust and Satisfaction: Patients are
more likely to trust and be satisfied with healthcare
providers who adhere to high standards of care.
Clear communication, patient education, and perso-
nalized care foster a positive healthcare experience,
encouraging patients to adhere to their treatment
regimens and engage actively in their care.

CONCLUSION

The NABH guidelines on rational prescription
and safe dispensing play a crucial role in ensuring
patient safety and improving healthcare quality. By
promoting evidence-based prescribing, comprehensive
documentation, qualified dispensing personnel, and
patient education, these guidelines help to minimize
medication errors and optimize patient outcomes.
Adherence to these standards not only enhances the
efficiency and effectiveness of healthcare delivery but
also builds patient trust and satisfaction, ultimately
contributing to better health outcomes and a more
robust healthcare system.

10.4 Additional Guidelines for Rational Use of
Ayurvedic Formulations

Rational drug use encompasses administering the
appropriate medication to the right patient, in the correct
dose, at the proper time, through the suitable route, and
in an economically feasible manner. The World Health
Organization (WHO) defines it as ensuring patients
receive medications suitable for their clinical needs,
at adequate doses, for the necessary duration, and at
minimal cost to both them and their community :

1. Safety and Effectiveness: Drugs should be chosen
based on their safety profile and proven efficacy
for the patient's condition, considering factors like
disease severity and available treatment options.

2. Appropriateness: This involves prescribing drugs for
their approved indications, at the correct dosage,
and ensuring proper dispensing and duration of
treatment. Patient counseling is also crucial for
understanding medication use.

3. Economic Considerations: Rational drug use
doesn’t just focus on price but also considers cost-
effectiveness. It aims to minimize expenses for both
the patient and the community while providing
optimal treatment.

APPROACHES TO ACHIEVING RATIONAL DRUG USE

1. Patient Evaluation: Understanding the patient's
medical history, including past illnesses and
medication usage, is essential for accurate diagnosis
and treatment planning.

----- PAGE 275 -----
Chapter 10 « Rational Prescription along with Safe Dispensing of Ayurvedic Fo

2. Diagnosis: Accurate diagnosis is fundamental for
rational therapy. It relies on comprehensive assess-
ments, including laboratory findings, to identify the
underlying causes of the patient's condition.

. Therapeutic Objectives: Treatment goals may include
symptom relief, disease prevention, oracombination
of both, depending on the patient's needs.

. Treatment Options: Treatment may involve
medication, lifestyle changes, or a combination.
When medication is necessary, the selection should
prioritize drugs with proven efficacy, safety,
suitability, cost-effectiveness, ease of administration,
and appropriate storage requirements.

Initiating Treatment: Once a drug is prescribed, it
should be administered as directe. Patient education
is crucial, informing them about both the benefits and
potential side effects of the medication. Patients should
also be equipped with knowledge on how to manage
any side effects that may occur. Planning a follow-up
visit allows for the assessment of treatment progress.

. Assessing Treatment Results: Evaluation of treatment
efficacy involves physical examination and
laboratory investigations. If the patient responds
positively to the therapy, it is deemed rational. If
not, the process returns to step 1 to reassess the
patient's condition.

7. Concluding Therapy: The success of therapy is
determined by assessing whether therapeutic goals
were achieved and if patient problems were resolve.
If these criteria aren’t met, factors such as patient
compliance and diagnostic accuracy should be re-
evaluated.

This structured approach ensures that treatment
decisions are continually reviewed and adjusted as
needed, optimizing patient outcomes and promoting
rational drug use. By adhering to these principles
and approaches, healthcare providers can ensure that
patients receive optimal therapy tailored to their clinical
needs while also considering economic factors and
minimizing the risks associated with medication use.

an

DRUG USE PROCESS INDICATORS
To ensure optimal drug therapy and rational drug use,
several key steps need to be followed:

1. Indication: Ensure there is a clear and appropriate
indication for its use before prescribing a drug.
Address all medical problems therapeutically.

2. Drug Selection: Choose the most suitable drug
based on its ability to achieve therapeutic goals,
considering patient variables, formulary status, and
therapy cost.

3. Regimen Selection: Determine the most appropriate
drug regimen that accomplishes therapeutic goals
at the least cost without compromising effectiveness
or causing toxicity.

4, Drug Provision: Facilitate the dispensing and supply
Process to ensure accurate preparation, dispensing
in ready-to-administer form, and timely delivery to
the patient.

5. Drug Administration: Ensure that appropriate devices
and techniques are used for drug administration
to optimize effectiveness and minimize adverse
effects.

6. Monitoring: Regularly monitor drug therapy
for effectiveness and adverse effects. Based on
monitoring results, decide whether to maintain,
modify, or discontinue the therapy.

7. Patient Counselling: Provide thorough counselling
and education to the patient or caregiver about
the prescribed therapy to ensure proper use of
medicines.

8. Effectiveness Evaluation: Evaluate the effectiveness of
the patient’s drug therapy by reviewing all previous
steps of the drug use process. Take appropriate
steps to ensure that therapeutic goals are achieved.

By diligently following these steps, healthcare profes-
sionals can ensure that drug therapy is rational,
effective, safe, and economical, ultimately leading to
improved patient outcomes.

41.1 Introduction to Traditional and Local Health
Practices and Government Initiatives to preserve it

INTRODUCTION
Traditional and local health practices have been integral
to human societies for centuries, embodying a wealth
of knowledge passed down through generations.
These practices encompass a variety of healing
methods, including herbal medicine, acupuncture,
Ayurveda, traditional Chinese medicine (ICM),
indigenous healing, and many others. They are often
deeply embedded in the cultural and spiritual lives of
communities, offering holistic approaches to health and
well-being. Governments worldwide have recognized
the importance of preserving these practices, launching
various initiatives to ensure their survival and
integration into contemporary healthcare systems.

UNDERSTANDING TRADITIONAL AND LOCAL HEALTH PRACTICES

1. Definition and Scope:

Traditional health practices refer to health knowledge,

skills, and practices based on the theories, beliefs, and

experiences indigenous to different cultures. They
include:

¢ Herbal Medicine: Use of plant-based substances for
therapeutic purposes.

~ Ayurveda: An ancient Indian system of medicine
focused on balance within the body and with nature.

* Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM): Encompasses
acupuncture, herbal medicine, and Qigong,
emphasizing harmony within the body.

% Indigenous Healing Practices: Vary widely but often
include spiritual healing, shamanism, and the use of
local herbs.

2. Importance in Contemporary Health Systems:

Traditional and local health practices are crucial for
several reasons:

1 / PRACTICES & TKDL

~ Accessibility: Often more accessible and affordable,
especially in rural or low-income areas.

& Cultural Relevance: Align with the cultural and
spiritual beliefs of the communities, enhancing
acceptance and adherence.

Holistic Approach: Focus on overall well-being,
including mental, emotional, and spiritual health.

BENEFITS OF TRADITIONAL AND LOCAL HEALTH PRACTICES

1. Holistic and Preventive Care: Traditional practices
often emphasize preventive care and holistic
health, addressing not just physical ailments but
also emotional and spiritual aspects. For example,
Ayurveda and TCM focus on maintaining balance
and preventing disease.

2. Biodiversity and Sustainable Use: These practices
promote the use of local plants and natural reso-
urces, contributing to biodiversity conservation and
sustainable practices. They also preserve valuable
ethnobotanical knowledge.

3. Empowerment and Community Involvement:
Traditional health practices empower communities
by valuing their knowledge and promoting self-
reliance in healthcare. This can strengthen social
cohesion and cultural identity.

4. Complementary Role in Modern Medicine: When
integrated with modern healthcare, traditional
practices can complement conventional treatments,
enhancing their effectiveness and patient satis-
faction. For instance, acupuncture is widely used to
manage pain and side effects of chemotherapy.

CHALLENGES IN PRESERVING TRADITIONAL AND LOCAL HEALTH
PRACTICES

1. Scientific Validation: A major challenge is the lack of
rigorous scientific validation for many traditional
practices, which can hinder their acceptance and
integration into main stream healthcare.

India to document and protect traditional knowledge,
particularly in the domains of Ayurveda, Unani,
Siddha, and Yoga. The project aims to prevent the
misappropriation of India’s rich traditional knowledge

by creating a comprehensive database that can be

accessed and used to challenge patent applications that
attempt to wrongly claim such knowledge as novel
inventions.

Website: www.tkdLres.in

OBJECTIVES OF TKDL

1. Protection of Traditional Knowledge: TKDL seeks to
protect traditional knowledge from biopiracy and
misappropriation by documenting it in a stand-
ardized format that is accessible to international
patent offices.

2. Promotion of Traditional Knowledge: By documenting
and digitizing traditional knowledge, TKDL
promotes the use and appreciation of India’s
cultural heritage on a global platform.

3. Facilitation of Research and Development: The
database serves as a valuable resource for res-
earchers and practitioners of traditional medicine,
encouraging innovation and the development of
new therapies.

KEY FEATURES OF TKDL

1. Comprehensive Database: TKDL contains detailed
information on traditional medicinal formulations,
practices, and texts. It translates this knowledge into
multiple languages, including English, German,
French, Spanish, and Japanese, making it accessible
to a wider audience.

2. Collaboration with Patent Offices: TKDL collaborates
with major international patent offices to prevent
the grant of erroneous patents. It provides evidence
from its database to refute patent claims that lack
novelty or involve traditional knowledge.

3. Multi-Disciplinary Approach: The project involves
experts from various fields, including traditional
medicine practitioners, scientists, and information
technology professionals, to ensure accurate and
comprehensive documentation.

4. User-Friendly Interface: The digital library is
designed to be user-friendly, allowing easy access to
documented traditional knowledge for researchers,
patent examiners, and other stakeholders.

IMPACT OF TKDL

1. Preventing Biopiracy; TKDL has _ successfully
challenged and prevented several patent applic-

ations based on traditional knowledge, thereby
safeguarding India’s intellectual property.

. Global Recognition: The initiative has gained global

recognition for its innovative approach to protecting
traditional knowledge, serving as a model for other
countries.

. Encouraging Ethical Research: By providing a legi-

timate source of traditional knowledge, TKDL
encourages ethical research and development,
ensuring that benefits derived from traditional
knowledge are shared fairly with communities that
have preserved it.

TRADITIONAL KNOWLEDGE DIGITAL LIBRARY (TKDL) FOR INDIAN
SYSTEMS OF MEDICINE

ig

The TKDL project involves experts from various
fields including Traditional Medicine (such as
Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, and Yoga), patent
examiners, IT specialists, scientists, and technical
officers.

_ TKDL serves as a crucial link between traditional

knowledge documented in local languages
and patent examiners at Intellectual Property
Offices (IPOs).

. By 2010, TKDL had transcribed 148 books on

Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, and Yoga, resulting in a
vast repository of 34 million pages of information.

. The information transcribed in the TKDL has been

translated into five languages: English, German,
French, Spanish, and Japanese, making it accessible
to a wider audience.

. Data on a significant number of formulations has

been included in the TKDL: 80,000 in Ayurveda,
1,000,000 in Unani, and 12,000 in Siddha.

. The TKDL integrates traditional knowledge with

modern systems, facilitating its preservation,
accessibility, and recognition on a global scale.

. This initiative helps prevent the misappropriation

of traditional knowledge by ensuring that it is
accessible to patent examiners, thus safe guarding
the rights of traditional knowledge holders.

. The success of TKDL highlights the importance

of collaboration between different stakeholders
including traditional medicine practitioners,
government agencies, and technical experts.

Data Storage: The knowledge extracted from ancient

. Translation: The stored information is translated into

proprietary system.

BENEFITS OF TKDL
1, Combatting Bio piracy: TKDL has successfully

identified 1,000 cases of biopiracy of India’s
traditional knowledge (IK) in the last three years.
Out of these, patent claims were withdrawn or
cancelled in 105 cases by the respective patent
offices. This is achieved at no cost to India and
within a significantly shorter time frame compared
to traditional legal battles.

. Cost and Time Efficiency: TKDL eliminates the need

for spending large sums of money and time in
legal battles against bio piracy. For instance, the
Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export
Development Authority (APEDA) spent 7 years and
Rs 7.62 crore in legal fees to fight for the intellectual
property rights of basmati rice.

. Decline in Patent Claims: There has been a notable

decline of up to 44% in patent claims filed on Indian
systems of medicine, indicating the effectiveness of
TKDL in preventing wrongful patenting.

. Inclusion of Yoga Postures: TKDL has expanded its

database to include videos of the most common yoga
postures. This addition helps prevent the wrongful
granting of patents for yoga exercises in the West,
addressing an increasing trend in misappropriation
of traditional knowledge.

4. Importance of Traditional and Local Health Practices
e Include herbal medicine, Ayurveda, traditional
Chinese medicine (TCM), and indigenous healing.
Offer holistic health solutions addressing physical,
mental, and spiritual well-being.
e More accessible and culturally relevant,
particularly in rural and low-income areas.
e Contribute to biodiversity conservation and
community empowerment.
e Complement modern medical treatments.
2. Challenges in Preservation
e Scientific Validation: Lack of rigorous scientific
validation.
e Standardization and Regulation: Variability in
preparation and use.
e Intellectual Property: Protecting rights and
ensuring fair benefit-sharing.
e Knowledge Erosion: Risk of losing traditional
knowledge due to globalization.
3. Government Initiatives
e Policy Development and Regulatory Frameworks:
e Establish national policies and legal frameworks.
e Examples: China’s integration of TCM, India’s
Ministry of AYUSH.

and CCRUM.

ational agreements like the Nagoya Protocol.
¢ Promotion and Awareness Campaigns.

Health” campaign).

events (e.g., International Day of Yoga).

Introduction

TKDL is an initiative by the Government of India
to document and protect traditional knowledge in
Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, and Yoga.

Objective: Prevent misappropriation of India’s tradi-
tional knowledge by creating a comprehensive, acce-
ssible database to challenge wrongful patent claims.

PHARMACOVIGILANCE FOR
AYURVEDA DRUGS

42.1 Introduction

Pharmacovigilance is a crucial aspect of clinical research,
involving the detection, assessment, understanding,
and prevention of adverse effects of medicines, both
short-term and long-term. It encompasses clinical trial
safety and post-marketing surveillance throughout a
product's lifecycle.

In India, pharmacovigilance is still developing, with
limited knowledge and progress compared to western
countries. Understanding its importance and impact
on the product lifecycle is essential for integrating
good practices, ensuring regulatory compliance, and
enhancing safety.

Pharmacovigilance aims to reduce the risk of drug-
related harms to patients. In India, the National
Pharmacovigilance Program, initiated in 2003 under the
Central Drug Standards Control Organization (CDSCO),
focuses on this goal. The WHO has emphasized
including traditional medicines in pharmacovigilance
systems and published guidelines on safety monitoring
of herbal medicines in 2004.

Etymology: The word ‘pharmaco’ comes from the
Greek ‘pharmacon’, meaning medicine, and ‘vigilance’
comes from the Latin ‘vigilantia’, meaning alertness
and attentiveness. Pharmacovigilance is about being
absolutely alert and watchful about the medicines we
give to patients.

Definition: Pharmacovigilance is the science and
activities related to detecting, assessing, understanding,
and preventing adverse effects or any other medicine-
related problems. It aims to ensure the safety and
effectiveness of medications, protecting patients from
harm and improving public health outcomes.

12.2 Important Terminology

Adverse Drug Reaction: ‘a response to a medicine which
is noxious and unintended, and which occurs at dose

normally used in man.’ or ‘any response to a drug that is
Noxious and unintended and that occurs at doses used
inman for prophylaxis, diagnostic or therapy, excluding
failure to accomplish the intended purpose.

Adverse Drug Event: ‘any untoward medical occurrence
that may present during treatment with a medicine, but
which does not necessarily have a causal relationship
with the treatment.’

Side Effect: Side effect is any unintended effect of a
pharmaceutical product occurring at doses normally
used in human which is related to the pharmacological
properties of the drug.

In Classical Ayurveda also prescribes metals and
minerals as medicines given as bhasmas or in combin-
ation with plants as herbo-mineral formulations (e.g.
Arogyavardhini).

12.3 History

* Thalidomide tragedy: 1960, German + 46 countries,
More than 20,000 affected- phocomelia.

+ India: On November 22, 2010, Hrithik Roshan
experienced an allergic reaction to antibiotics,
resulting in spasms in his lungs and throat.

2. Benoxaprofen (NSAID): Year of Marketing: - 1982,

- Liver Necrosis.

National Pharmacovigilance Programme for ASU

Drugs (NPP-ASU) The National Pharmacovigilance

Programme for Ayurveda, Siddha, and Unani (ASU)

drugs was initiated in December 2007, following a

workshop sponsored by the World Health Organization

(WHO) at IPGT and RA, Jamnagar, to explore the

implementation of pharmacovigilance for ASU

drugs. The protocol and adverse drug reaction (ADR)
reporting forms were developed and discussed by the

Department of Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani,

Siddha, and Homoeopathy (AYUSH), Government of

India, in August 2008. The final draft was released by

the Department of AYUSH on September 29, 2008. Since

then, IPGT and RA, Jamnagar, India, has served as the

National Pharmacovigilance Resource Centre for ASU

drugs in India.

Furthermore, on January 20, 2005, Schedule Y of the

Drugs and Cosmetics Act (DCA) was comprehensively

amended to include extensive pharmacovigilance

obligations for companies intending to manufacture
and market new drugs in India.

NEED OF PV IN ASU

In ancient times, Ayurvedic physicians prepared
medicines for their patients themselves. However,
today, this practice is followed by only a handful of
practitioners, as the production and sale of Ayurvedic
drugs have evolved into a formalized and thriving
industry. The manufacture and marketing of Ayurvedic
drugs are regulated by the Drugs and Cosmetics
Act, 1940.

Broadly, two categories of medicines labelled as
“Ayurvedic” are available in the market: Classical
Ayurvedic formulations, which adhere to descriptions
in Ayurveda samhitas (e.g., kutajarishta), and patentand
proprietary formulations made from herbal extracts.
There are 8,403 licensed Ayurvedic pharmacies, and
the industry’s approximate turnover is Rs. 4,000 crore,
accounting for nearly a third of the total pharmaceutical
business in India.
However, this commercialization has brought challenges
regarding the safe use of Ayurvedic medicines,
emphasizing the need for formal pharmacovigilance
programs in the field. Despite this, the number of
adverse reactions to Ayurvedic drugs reported or
recorded in the National Pharmacovigilance Program
in India is negligible. This is largely attributed to the
strong belief that Ayurvedic medicines are safe.
WHO CAN REPORT AN ADR?

1. Clinician

2. Nurses/ Drug Provider

3. Consumers

4. Pharmacist

5. Pharmaceutical Company.

BENEFITS OF PHARMACOVIGILANCE (PV)

1. Provides information about adverse drug reactions

(ADRs) to the general population.

- Knowledge of adverse effects helps in effective
treatment.

3. Helps to detect rare ADRs that may not be identified
in pre-marketing surveillance.

. Aids in collecting comprehensive data on ADRs
from all sections of society, including various
diseases and dietary traditions, which may not be
included in pre-marketing surveillance.

. Facilitates the development of a better system for
reporting ADRs.

ROLE OF PHARMACOVIGILANCE

1. Identifying, quantifying, and documenting drug-
related problems.

2. Contributing to reducing the risk of drug-related
problems in the healthcare system.

3. Increasing knowledge and understanding of factors
and mechanisms responsible for drug-related
injuries.

Pharmacovigilance is essential for ensuring the
safety, quality, and efficacy of drugs by identifying,
assessing, ensuring, and minimizing harmful effects, It
benefits society and the healthcare system by boosting
confidence in drug safety, ensuring the safety of drugs
to minimize adverse effects, and maintaining drug
efficacy to provide maximum benefit to patients.
Note: Schedule Y of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act (DCA) of
1945, which addresses drug safety, was thoroughly
amended on January 20, 2005. This amendment

275

introduced detailed pharmacovigilance obligations
for companies aiming to manufacture and market
new drugs in India.

SCHEDULE Y OF THE DRUGS AND COSMETICS AcT INCLUDES

REGULATIONS ON

* Preclinical and clinical studies for developing
new drugs.

* Clinical trial requirements for importing drugs.

* Manufacturing and obtaining marketing approvals
for new drugs in India.

* The continued commitment of the DCGI (Drugs
Controller General of India) to ensure pharmaceutical
companies comply with pharmacovigilance
obligations.

+ Clear responsibilities for pharmaceutical companies
regarding their marketed products and reporting
adverse events from clinical trials.

Central Sector Scheme and Centres of Pharmaco-
vigilance of ASU & H Drugs

The Central Sector Scheme for promoting
pharmacovigilance of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, and
Homoeopathy (ASU&H) drugs is an initiative by the
Ministry of AYUSH, Government of India. The scheme
aims to monitor the safety of traditional medicine
products and detect any adverse reactions or side
effects.
The Centres of Pharmacovigilance are institutions
established under this scheme to collect, analyze,
and disseminate information related to adverse drug
reactions (ADRs) of ASU&H drugs. These centers are
responsible for:

1. Monitoring and reporting ADRs

2 Conducting pharmacovigilance activities

3. Providing safety information to healthcare
professionals and consumers

4. Collaborating with national and international
pharmacovigilance agencies

The main objectives of the scheme are:

1. To establish a robust pharmacovigilance system for
ASU&H drugs

2 To ensure the safe use of traditional medicine
products

3. To promote rational use of ASU&H drugs

4. To contribute to the global pharmacovigilance
efforts.

APPENDICES

1, PANCHVIDHA KASHAYA KALPANA

The term “Panchavidha Kashaya Kalpana” describes
five fundamental methods for making herbal remedies.
These techniques seek to improve the medication’s
efficacy, palatability, and shelf life. It includes:

]. Svarasa Kalpana

2. Kalka Kalpana

3. Kvatha Kalpana

4, Hima Kalpana

5. Phanta Kalpana

4.1 Svarasa Kalpana

In Ayurveda, juice (Svarasa) is the liquid extract of fresh,
clean, green herbs obtained by squeezing, pressing, or
using any tool. This juice is fresh.

| 4.2 Kalka Kalpana

Herbal paste, often referred to as Kalka, is a paste created
by crushing and grinding fresh herbs. It also contains a
paste composed of water and dry herbs. It is also known
as Aavapa or Prakshepa. Nonetheless, herbal paste is
referred to be Prakshepa if it is prepared by combining
ghee, oil, or any other sour ingredient.

| 1.3 Kvatha Kalpana

The concoction made by boiling one part herbs in
sixteen parts water until it is reduced to one-eighth part
water is called a kvatha.

| 1.4 Hima Kalpana

In Ayurveda, the water obtained by soaking one part of
herbs in six parts of water for the entire night, followed
by cleaning and filtering in the morning, is called a cold
infusion, or Hima.

APPENDIX-I : BRIEF INTRODUCTION OF CLASSICAL DOSES FORM AND
THEIR METHOD OF PREPARATION

1.5 Phanta Kalpana

Phanta is the term for the water that remains after
adding hot water to herbs. Ratio of drug water is 1:4.

Shelf life: Instant Use (Saviryatavadhi)
2. CHURANA KALPANA

Churna is a dried form of Kalka Kalpana, often used
to create Kalka. It refers to the powdered form of a
single drug or a mixture of two or more drugs that
have been powdered separately and then blended
homogeneously. According to the Indian Ayurvedic
formulary, Churna is a fine powder of medication or
drug mixture. Sharngadhara lists synonyms for Chura
as raja or kshoda, and it is administered in the dose
of one karsha-parmana. Acharya Kashyapa describes
Churna as a fine powder used for treating grahani-roga
(digestive disorders), ama vikara (toxicity disorders),
vrana (wounds), and as an anjana (collyrium for eyes).
Acharya Sushruta also emphasizes the importance of
Churna Kalpana in treatment, as noted in the Ashtanga
Sameraha and Ashtanga Hridaya. The use of Churna ~
Kalpana continues to increase over time. 4

3. VATI KALPANA
Vati Kalpana, as described in Ayurveda, is a potent
and stable dosage form that is extensively detailed in
the Sharngadhara Samhita. Acharya Sharngadhara has

included various forms like Guda (jaggery), Gutika

(pills), Vati (tablets), Pindi, Modaka, and Guggulu under

the single heading of Vati in one chapter, showcasing

their significance and versatility in Ayurvedic medicine.

Binding agents are crucial in the preparation of Vatj

formulations. The primary binding agents used include:
1. Guda (Jaggery)

. Sita (Sugar)

. Guggulu

. Madhu (Honey)

. Gomutra (Cow Urine)

. Svarasa (Fresh Juice)

. Kvatha (Decoction)

ND OF & WwW NO

THESE AGENTS SERVE MULTIPLE PURPOSES

1. Consistency: When subjected to heat, these binding

agents melt and achieve the consistency of Avaleha

(a semi-solid form). This ensures the powdered
herbs mix thoroughly and bind well.

2. Hardness and Friability: The sticky nature of these
agents provides the Vati with the required hardness
and reduces friability, ensuring the tablets do not
break easily.

3. Therapeutic Benefits: Many of these agents, such
as Guggulu and Gomutra, have their therapeutic
properties that complement the medicinal effects of
the herbs used.

PREPARATION PROCESS
The preparation process involves several steps to ensure
the stability and efficacy of the Vati:

1. Heating and Melting: Guda is often heated alone
or mixed in Kvatha and then heated. This melted
Guda is then mixed with the herbal powders.

2. Bhavana Dravya: Gomutra, Svarasa, and Kvatha are
used as Bhavana Dravya (wetting agents), which
act as binding agents when Guda, Sita, and Madhu
are not used. These agents help in faster dispersion
of the Vati due to their inability to achieve Avaleha
consistency.

3. Mixing and Cooling: The herbal mixture is added
to the melted binding agent and mixed properly.
Once the mixture cools down, it is shaped into Vati,
ensuring proper hardness and reduced friability.

TYPES OF VATI AND THEIR FORMULATION

Various formulations and their specific characteristics
are outlined by Acharya Sharngadhara:

Guggulu Formulations: Guggulu is melted, herbal
powders are added, and the mixture is shaped into

----- PAGE 295 -----
Appendices :
Pindakriti form and then into Gutika (pills) using
mechanical force (Kuttana).

Modaka: Typically made of 1 Pala (4 Tola).

sanjivani Vati: Made up of 1 Gunja.

THERAPEUTIC INDICATIONS AND BENEFITS

Acharya Sharngadhara’s choice of binding agents
like Guda, Guggulu, and Gomutra was not random.
These agents were selected not only for their binding
properties but also for their therapeutic benefits:

Guda: Known for its demulcent properties and used to
treat conditions like cough and hoarseness of voice.
Guggulu: Renowned for its anti-inflammatory and lipid-

lowering effects.
Gomutra: Used forits detoxifying and diuretic properties.

VARIATIONS IN DOSAGE

The dosage of Vati formulations varies due to several

factors:

1, Characteristics of Dispersion: The choice of binding

agent affects how quickly the Vati disperses in

the body.

. Bioavailability: Different binding agents and
preparation methods impact the bioavailability of
the active ingredients.

3. Therapeutic Use: Depending on whether the Vati
is used for therapeutic purposes, as a Rasayana
(rejuvenative), or as a Vajikarana (aphrodisiac), the
dosage and formulation may vary.

Vati Kalpana represents a sophisticated approach
in Ayurvedic pharmaceutics, combining the art of
formulation with therapeutic efficacy. The detailed
procedures and thoughtful selection of ingredients
by Acharya Sharngadhara highlight the profound
understanding of herbal pharmacology and the
importance of dosage forms in achieving optimal
therapeutic outcomes.

4. GUGGULU KALPANA

Guggulu is a resin derived from Commiphoramukul,
a small tree known as Indian bedellium. The use of
guggulu is first documented in the Sushruta Samhita,
and it should be used one year after its collection.
Nava guggulu acts as a rasayana (rejuvenative), while
purana guggulu causes apakarshana (detoxification).
Pharmaceutically, guggulu is used as a binding agent in
the preparation of vati (tablets), in addition to its own
pharmacological properties. Bhava Mishra describes
five types of guggulu; the hiranyakshya variety should
be used for humans, while other varieties are for
veterinary purposes.

N

Guggulu is a suffix in many preparations, indicatin
suggulu kalpana (formulations) and its pi
quantity, such as in Yogaraja guggulu, Kaishora
guggulu, and Trayodasanga guggulu. Guggulu is also
an ingredient in many pharmaceutical forms, including
vati, gutika, rasa kriya, kvatha, dhupa, churna
taila, ghrita, avaleha, and modaka. It is also used in
preparations such as rasausadhies, lepa, and pradeha.
In the A.EL., Part I, Second Revised English Edition, by
the Government of India, Ministry of Health and Family
Welfare, Dept. of I. S. M. and H. New Delhi, we find
the authentic use of the following liquids for svedana
in ‘Dolayantra’:

1, Gomutra (cow’s urine)

2. Vasapatra svarasa or kashaya

3. Nirgundi svarasa with Haridra churna

GENERAL METHOD OF PREPARATION OF GUGGULU KALPANA
WITH AGNI

1. One part of purified guggulu and one part of
dravya churna (powdered ingredients) are mixed
for the preparation of guggulu kalpana.

2. Shodhita (purified) guggulu should be mixed with
the prescribed quantity of water and prepared
as paka by heating, similar to guda paka (jaggery
preparation).

3. It is then mixed with the powders of the prescribed
ingredients with constant stirring and rolled into
vati form by adding a small quantity of ghee to
maintain the soft consistency of the guggulu and to
prevent it from sticking to the hands while rolling
the pills.

WITHOUT AGNI

1. Shuddha guggulu is pounded rigorously, either
manually or ina pounding machine, by adding fine
powder of medicinal drugs little by little.

2. When all the medicinal drugs are evenly
incorporated into the guggulu and the mixture
turns smoother with the required consistency for
rolling the pills, the pills of desired size and shape
are rolled.

3. These pills are dried in the shade and stored in
airtight containers for further therapeutic use.

4. Nowadays, guggulu preparations are manufactured
using modern tablet methodologies.

7. ASAVA ARISHTA

DEFINITION

Asavas and Arishtas are medicinal preparations. It is
made by soaking drugs in powder form or decoction
(kashaya) in a solution of sugar or jaggery. It undergo
fermentation, generating alcohol. Alcohol facilitates
extraction of active principles and acts as a preservative.
METHOD OF PREPARATION

Arishta

1. Drugs are coarsely powdered and kashaya is
prepared.

2. Kashaya is strained and placed in a
fermentation vessel.

3. Sugar, jaggery, or honey is dissolved, boiled,
filtered, and added.

4. Prakshepa dravyas are finely powdered and added.
5. Dhataki pushpa (if included) is cleaned and added.

6. Vessel is covered with an earthen lid and edges
sealed with clay-smeared cloth in seven layers.

7. Kept in a special room, underground cellar, or
paddy heap to maintain constant temperature.

8. After fermentation, lid is removed and contents
examined.

9. Fluid is decanted and strained after 2-3 days.

10. Strained again after fine particles settle and then
bottled.

Asava

1. Water and prescribed Jaggery or sugar are boiled
and cooled.

2. Poured into fermentation vessel.

3. Fine powder of drugs mentioned in the formula
is added.

8. BHASMA PRAKARANA

DEFINITION
Bhasma are calcined powder of metals, minerals, or
animal products, using cow dung cakes (puta).
METHOD OF PREPARATION

1. First Stage: Sodhana (Purification)

e Purpose: Eliminate harmful matter, modify
properties, convert characteristics, and enhance
therapeutic action.

Types:

e Samanya Shodhana: General purification (e.g.,
heating metal sheets, immersing in taila, takra,
gomutra).

e Vishesa Shodhana: Specific purification (e.g.,
bhavana, svedana, mardana).

2. Second Stage: Marana (Calcination)

e Preparation:

e Grind purified drug with plant juices or
kashayas.

¢ Form and sun-dry small cakes (chakrikas).

¢ Calcination:
¢ Seal cakes in earthen plates.
¢ Place ina pit filled with cow dung cakes, ignite,

cool, and grind into fine powder.

° Repetition: Repeat trituration, chakrikas making,
and puta process as needed.

9. PISHTI
DEFINITION
Medicines prepared by triturating the drug with
specified liquids and exposing it to sun or moonlight,
known as anagnitapta bhasma (bhasma prepared
without fire).
METHOD OF PREPARATION
1. Take Shodhita (Purified) drug.
2. The shodhita drug is placed ina khalva.
3. It is triturated with rose water (unless otherwise
specified) for a day.
4. The triturated drug is dried in the sun for
another day.
5. This process is repeated for seven days or more
until a fine powder, pisti, is obtained.
CHARACTERISTICS AND PRESERVATION
* Colour: Varies depending on the drug used.
“ Texture: As fineasbhasma, withsimilarcharacteristics.
+ Potency: Preserves potency indefinitely.
Storage: Stored in glass stoppered bottles.
10. KHARLIYA RASAYANA

Kharaliya Rasayana is one of the most commonly
utilized Parad Murchchhita Aushadha Vargikarana
formulations in Ayurveda, recommended extensively
across various disease conditions. The formulations that
are prepared in a Kharala (mortar) by triturating until
they attain the chief desired characteristics are known
as Kharaliya Rasayana. It is a common dosage form in
Ayurvedic medicine, containing metals and minerals,
and is widely used in clinical practice. The principles
of Bhavana and Mardana Samskara form the backbone

----- PAGE 298 -----
284

Rasashastra and Bhaishajya Kalpana

of Kharaliya Rasayana preparation, ensuring both its
therapeutic efficacy and safety. Bhavana, a Samskara
process, alters the original properties of raw drugs,
inducing new ones in the main drugs. Mardana and
Bhavana Samskara play a pivotal role in ensuring the
intimate contact of material particles with the liquid
media, facilitating the impregnation of media properties
into the material, and transforming coarse powder intoa
finer state to aid further processing. This process results
in unique and suitable physico-chemical changes that
enhance the efficacy of the material. The Mardana and
Bhavana processes thus contribute significantly to the
production of quality medicines, particularly Kharaliya
Rasayana. Kharaliya Rasayana, prepared in classical
ways, is both safe and effective for clinical practice in
therapeutic doses.

11. PARPATI KALPANA
Liquefied Kajjali is poured over neatly arranged mocha
patra (shalmali patra) or another suitable leaf to create
a thin wafer (papada). This method, called pota bandha
of parada, produces Parpati.
METHOD OF PREPARATION
1. Triturate purified mercury and sulphur to make
Kajjali.
2. Mix other ingredients in the khalva.
3. Heat the mixture in an iron vessel using a
Sikata yantra.
4. Line a pit in cow dung with a leaf.
5. Pour the melted medicine onto the leaf.

6. Cover with another leaf and press gently with
cow dung.

7. Allow to cool.
8. Powder the cooled medicine for use.

12. KUPIPAKVA KALPANA
Kupipakva rasayana refers to formulations created by
applying specific heat to purified mercury (shuddha
parada), purified sulphur (shuddha gandhaka), and
other rasadravya in a chosen glass bottle, following
the distinctive preparation method outlined in
traditional texts.
GENERAL METHOD OF PREPARATION
Purva Karma

1. Collect all the essential equipments (Raw material,
Kupi, Kapada Mitti, Valuka Yantra, Shita shalaka,
Tapta Shalaka, Pyrometer, etc.).

Pradhana Karma

1. Shuddha parada and shuddha gandhaka are
triturated continuously in a khalva yantra for 4
to 5 days.

2. The resulting kajjali may undergo bhavana with
any mentioned bhavana dravya.

3. Metallic foils like svarnapatra, if included, are
carefully cut into smaller pieces and added to the
khalva yantra.

4. Equal quantities of shuddha parada are then added
to the mixture and triturated rigorously for 4 to 5
days until a fine drug paste is obtained.

5. The resulting drug mass is then triturated with the
specified quantity of gandhaka for 2 to 3 days.

6. Optionally, this kajjali_may undergo further
bhavana.

7. The bhavita kajali is carefully collected and filled
into a bottle (Kupi).

8. Seven layers of mritvastralepana must be applied
to the bottle.

Appendices

9, Ensure that only % to 1/3 of the bottle is filled with
kajjali.
10. Temporarily close the mouth of the bottle with a
cork and firmly place it in the Valuka yantra.

Pashchat Karma

1. Kupi Uddharana

2. Kupi Bhedana

13. POTTALI KALPANA

Pottali Kalpana is a consolidated form of mercurial
preparation incorporating the Pota Bandha of Parada.
Pottali is a type of preparation that results from Parada
Murchhana, a procedure where mercury is thoroughly
ground with other herbo-mineral drugs to enhance its
therapeutic efficiency.
GENERAL METHOD OF POTTALI KALPANA

1. Bhavana Samskara

e Purify, process, and incinerate (if adding Bhasma)
all ingredients.

e Finely powder the ingredients.

Subject the powdered ingredients to Bhavana ina
Khalva Yantra with herbal liquid media (usually
Kumari pulp if unspecified).

e Continue Bhavana until the mixture is viscous
and semisolid.

e Repeat the procedure 3 to 7 times, examining the
Subhavita Lakshana.

e Collect, dry, powder, and preserve the final
mixture.

2. Puta Paka Samskara

e Purify and incinerate metalo-mineral ingredients.

e Triturate with herbal media until uniform.

e Incinerate using techniques like Gaja Puta.

« Use Kaparda or Musha methods for specific
preparations.

3. Pottali Paka

e Select appropriate metals, minerals, and herbs.

e Use herbal extracts like Kumari Svarasa for
Bhavana.

Determine the Pottali shape (e.g. pyramid,
conical).

e Ensure proper drying of Pottali.

e Choose suitable storage containers.

15, LEPA KALPANA

About the Book :

Ayurvediya Aushadhi Prayoga Vigyana (Part-2 of Textbook of Rasashastra & Bhaishajya Kalpana) encompasses
twelve chapters, meticulously aligned with the latest NCISM syllabus for BAMS second professional, It Offers a
comprehensive exploration of the basic principles of Ayurvediya Aushadhi Prayoga Vigyana, explained with clear
scientific rationale with aims to enhance the understanding and application of Ayurvedic formulations, blending
traditional wisdom with modern scientific insights. Additionally, the inclusion of multiple-choice questions (MCQs)
at the end of each chapter is designed to boost students’ confidence and ability to tackle examinations effectively.
The English edition of this bookis set to broaden the reach and impact of this field of knowledge, making it accessible
to a wider audience. We trust that this textbook will be an invaluable resource for everyone in the field of Ayurveda,
particularly for B.A-M.S. students and those Preparing for P.G. entrance examinations as well as P.G. students,
